Below the gallery, past six hours of cold soak, the pump vault: a flooded chamber holding
the exchanger intakes, the pumps that keep the gallery dry, and the cradle with the original
Kestrel core drowned on it. It has been under brine since the year of the exchanger fire and
nothing in it has been dry since.

It is eleven metres from the inner door of the soak lock - the throat - to the core cradle,
and those eleven metres are the whole world of any scene set here. There is no guide line
strung across them, because a line in a working vault fouls the intakes, and the co-op
stopped replacing them. There is no fixed lamp, because a fixed lamp in this water lights a
sphere four metres wide and costs a pump's worth of power to do it. A diver crosses by
counting, by the pitch of the intakes, and by knowing which way the current off the
exchangers pushes her.

The cradle itself is a steel yoke on four feet, bolted through to the ice, and it rings. When
the shelf works overhead the whole vault takes the note and the cradle holds it longest,
which is how a diver with her hand on it knows the surface is moving before she knows
anything else.

The throat is the only way in or out. Everything else in this room is intake, and an intake
is a hole that does not let a person through.
